dataKinds.name: Harmonised observations (P1 allele counts each fit consumes)
dataKinds.location: Built in memory by the adapters in genomeos/observations/sources/ (map_surveys, map_g6pd, afnd_frequencies, afnd_cytokines, afnd_carriers, gnomad_hgdp_1kg, wbbc, publications) from raw inputs at fit time. A store writer exists (genomeos/observations/ingest.py: hive-partitioned chrom=*/part-0.parquet, read with DuckDB), but fitting is not wired to it yet (refit design non-goal, 'gap 3'). Persisted copies: (a) one observations JSON per published artifact in the web bucket (atlas/web/downloads/<id>/<model>/<data>/<id>.observations.<sha16>.json); (b) the frozen HbS parity input at validation/hbs-piel-parity-2026-09-16/ in the data store.
dataKinds.format: In memory: pandas validated by pandera (strict, coerce). On disk: parquet (the parity input; ingest.py layout), JSON (web).
dataKinds.schema: OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA, 17 columns, strict, no defaults: variant_id (regex chr-pos-ref-alt GRCh38 | phenotype: | hla:/kir:/mic:/cyt:), rsid (nullable), population_id, lat, lon, radius_km>0, ac Int64>=0, an Int64>0, source_record_id (unique, namespace:sha256), source, assay (genotype | enzyme_activity | frequency_reconstructed | genotype_counted | genome | ...), date_lower/date_upper Int64 years BP, sampling_design (7-value enum), disease_ascertainment_excluded (nullable boolean dtype, nulls refused), cohort_id, ingest_version. Checks: ac<=an, date_lower<=date_upper. KIR presence goes in a separate CARRIER_OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA (carriers/n_individuals instead of ac/an). The web JSON rows are a different projection: ac, an, assay, citation_text, cohort_id, disease_ascertainment_excluded, ingest_version, lat, lon, population_label, radius_km, sampling_design, source_locator, source_record_id, source_url, study_id, study_label. They have no population_id, rsid, source or date fields; variant_id is in the artifact header.
dataKinds.rowsNow: Web JSON: 9,273 rows across the 30 served artifacts (HbS 1,071; G6PD 910; HLA 194-419 each; KIR 233-235; cytokines 77-99). Parity parquet: 994 rows (385 cohorts, sum an 11,359,130, sum ac 175,878). Source capacity per adapter docstrings and the HF card: AFND 79,672 usable rows across 4,059 alleles and 1,477 populations (from a 123,502-row harvest); MAP HbS 1,287 raw surveys (1,071 used); MAP G6PD 1,749 raw (910 used); gnomAD HGDP+1KG 80 populations; WBBC 4 regions.
dataKinds.bytesNow: Web observations JSON: 7.15 MB decoded in total (e.g. hla-a-02-01 is 201,145 B decoded and 29,406 B gzip). Parity parquet 45,704 B plus TSV 170,914 B.
dataKinds.growth: P1 acceptance (design §15) adds gnomAD HGDP+1KG, AADR (ancient, dated; P6 fits it later), GAsP (219 populations), MCPS, IndiGen, GenomeIndia (99), H3Africa and Qatar, plus literature corpora. The LCT pilot holds 426 audited source rows; HBB and G6PD are next. Computed from stated numbers: the 698-variant curated candidate set times 80 HGDP+1KG populations is about 56K rows from gnomAD alone. Design §10/§11 call the observations layer 'whole genome, always available'. Read literally, that is 153M variants x 80 populations, about 1.2e10 rows: an upper bound, with no timeline stated. likelyQueries: All observations of variant V (ac, an, radius_km, sampling_design, cohort_id, assay, citation) whose disc lies within 500 km of (lat, lon), using great-circle distance and ideally the radius as well.

Value of every surface at one H3 cell or point (post_median, q025, q975, support, posterior_contraction, dist_nearest_obs_km) across all variants and all (model_version, data_version). This must map res 3 (v1/v2) to res 4 (v3) through h3 parent and child.

Observations for V joined to P0 populations (population_id to lat, lon, uncertainty_radius_km, location_type, provenance, biocultural_notice) with sampling_design and disease_ascertainment_excluded. Today the web JSON has no population_id, so the join falls back to population_label or cohort_id.
What changed between releases R1 and R2: objects added, removed, or with a changed sha256 or key reuse (a manifest diff; 2026-10-17 to 2026-10-18 added 3 parity files).

For one dataset, old versus new surface: per-cell Δmedian, z=Δmedian/√(sd_old²+sd_new²), 4x4 support transitions, the share of cells with sd_new>1.2·sd_old, and the WorldPop-weighted mean |Δmedian| (refit QC).
Observation diff between two data_versions of a dataset, broken down by source, sampling_design and cohort (rows added, removed or changed, keyed by source_record_id).
Population-weighted mean or sum of V over a country, admin unit or lasso polygon, excluding unknown and prior_dominated cells and returning the excluded fraction (/aggregate).
National burden totals computed draw by draw (sum the cells within a draw, then take quantiles), joined to the WorldPop res-4 grid, then compared with Piel 2013 IQRs.
Which variants have observed or supported cells in region X, and which H3 cells are unknown for every variant ('unstudied here' coverage gaps).
Every artifact version for V: which release first held it, which one is served now (the pin), and whether any key is in WITHDRAWN.json.
Exact inputs of artifact A for reproduction: input sha256s, registry_version, grid sha256, FitConfig, seed, git SHA and lock (planned served.json and provenance.json).
Does a derived (variant_id, model_version, data_version) key already exist in any committed release? This is the refit selection rule.
Counts of observations per variant by source, sampling_design and assay, for example how many clinical_case or convenience rows drive an HLA surface.
Sum of an (effective sample) within the correlation range of a cell; observations per population; populations in the registry with no observations.
Alias lookup: (source, label) to population_id. Populations within R km of a point, by location_type.
All HLA alleles at a locus observed in AFND population P, with reconstructed ac/an, plus the carrier frequency for KIR genes, which is kept separate.
Which published objects derive from a non_commercial or not_checked source (a manifest filter by sources and terms.status).
Top variants by post_median at a cell, restricted to supported cells; the distribution of posterior_contraction per variant (the reported prior_dominated fraction).
Later (P6): observations with date_lower/date_upper in a years-BP window, and time-sliced surfaces at a cell.
Website: fetch catalog, grid, render, detail and observations by key (no query; a pure key-value read).
constraints: Observations and surfaces are never conflated: separate tables, layers, keys and provenance. Allele counts (ac/an) and carrier counts (carriers/n_individuals) are separate tables too.
No inference on the serving path. Any query layer may only read and aggregate precomputed artifacts.
Counts, not frequencies: store ac and an, never ac/an. AFND and WBBC counts are reconstructions labelled in assay.

Schema violations are hard errors. No defaults for uncertainty_radius_km, sampling_design, disease_ascertainment_excluded or cohort_id. Strict pandera schemas with coercion that refuses non-integral counts.

Variant IDs come in several namespaces (chr-pos-ref-alt GRCh38, phenotype:, hla:, kir:, mic:, cyt:), so partitioning by chromosome alone does not fit every entity (ingest.py writes chrom=phenotype%3Ag6pd).

Artifacts are immutable, keyed (variant_id, model_version, data_version). A refit coexists with what it supersedes. Release keys are immutable and data/releases is append-only. Web keys are content-addressed, and nothing is overwritten or deleted. Takedown goes through WITHDRAWN.json plus an owner delete.

Reads need no credentials. The data-store bucket is read-by-key only (legacyObjectReader, no listing), so every key comes from the manifest. Open CORS on the data store; CORS on the web bucket is limited to the site origins.
fetch_data.py is standard library only, with sha256 verification and atomic rename. GPU pods with no cloud account must be able to read everything.

$200/month budget with alerts at 50/90/150% actual and 100% forecast. At 150% ($300) the kill switch removes public access from the data-store bucket only. The web bucket and other spend keep billing. Egress is about $0.12/GB, about $0.03 per full release download. Requester-pays was rejected because it breaks credential-free reads.
Pickles are never published. Object-dtype .npy is refused. Media types come from a closed table (.tif must be added deliberately). Files over about 150 MB risk composite uploads, which have no md5.

Terms are carried, not adjudicated: per-source status and non_commercial markers (GeneReviews; gnomAD-bundled SpliceAI fields; AlphaGenome top_attributions). Restricted sources such as All of Us may inform models but never be served.
No project ids, numbers, accounts or credentials in git. Only public bucket URLs and names may be committed.
Refit design (draft): no standing GCP resources, no credentials in any job that runs science code, WIF-only create-only upload, GitHub-hosted CPU runners, GCP-native compute rejected.

Design §3/§10 already chose DuckDB-on-Cloud-Run over parquet in GCS for interactive reads and BigQuery for batch (ingest staging, H3 rollups, GADM precomputation). Nothing on the interactive path may touch BigQuery.

Variant-class eligibility (Mendelian or CPIC only for burden) is enforced server-side in the API. The P12 agent's only tool surface is the P4 API, with no raw SQL; Pan-UKB MCP likewise excludes arbitrary SQL.
Aggregates must exclude unknown and prior_dominated cells and return the excluded fraction.
Web data format versioning: a MAJOR change publishes new keys, a MINOR change is additive only, and the catalog has no default version.

Surfaces are res-4 parquet with a string h3_index, a single row group, snappy, sorted by h3_index, about 7.5 MB per surface. Today's v3 surfaces share one 77,844-cell grid, and the web encoder refuses differing grids.
Determinism: SEED=42, byte-deterministic encoders, release builds and bundles.
openQuestions: Will the harmonised P1 observations become a published first-class table, for example the chrom-partitioned parquet in ingest.py? Today they exist only per artifact in the web JSON, plus one parity parquet, and fitting is not wired to the observation store.
Should the web observations JSON carry population_id, rsid, source and date fields, so that it joins to the registry and matches the P1 schema?

Will a P0 population registry release (populations.parquet, aliases, manifest with RELEASE+sha256 identity) be published? The served surfaces cite non-semver labels ('afnd-2026-08', 'map-survey-coordinates-v1').

Does 'observations layer: whole genome, always available' (design §10/§11) mean every variant in gnomAD HGDP+1KG (about 153M x 80, about 1.2e10 rows) or the curated set (698 candidates, about 56K rows)? The answer decides between files and a warehouse.
Which entities get fitted beyond the 30 served ones (the 698 curated candidates? all 4,059 AFND alleles?), at which resolutions, and when? The res 5/6 promotion thresholds are not calibrated.
Will posterior draw matrices (about 311 MB per variant at res 4, 500 draws) and burden layers be published, and in what layout?
What export format will fits use (#471: netCDF + JSON + npz), how large will the exports be, and will the public HF mirror keep serving pickles?
Phase 2 (#472) scope: publish the 870 MB WorldPop raster or only the res-4 grid? Publish the AFND page caches at all? Terms checks for WorldPop and project outputs are still not_checked.

Who exactly are the external SQL users, and is 'no account' a hard requirement? Any warehouse query service bills either the querier or the project, and the kill switch protects only the data-store bucket's egress.
Is BigQuery batch (design §3/§10) still intended now that the refit design runs fits on GitHub runners and rejected GCP-native compute?

Docs conflict on the cache lifetime of the 2026-10-17 objects: cost-controls.md says max-age=31536000 immutable; data-store.md and data_release.CACHE_CONTROL say 3600. This affects takedown and CDN behaviour for any query layer.
Refit cadence: event-driven only, or will scheduled re-harvesting be added? It is deferred, and there is no stated number of refits per month.

Will superseded artifact versions (v1/v2) stay in the full logical tree of every release manifest indefinitely, so that each manifest grows with every version?
Is the Pan-UKB PostgreSQL/Cloud SQL layer expected to share storage or query infrastructure with the Atlas, or stay separate?

options.name: Hash-pinned (Geo)Parquet on the public data-store bucket, read directly by DuckDB or Polars
options.kind: File-based lake that works on any cloud: the current data store, upgraded. No server and no reader account.
options.fit: The best fit for the AGENTS.md invariants, and it is what the repo already does. Release keys are immutable and sha256-pinned, the manifest is the record of truth, and the Parquet file is the citable artifact. Observations and surfaces stay in separate files. ac and an stay integer columns. There is no inference on the serving path. Today's corpus is small: the 2026-10-18 release has 248 objects and 271 MB, of which 266 MB is 62 Parquet files. One v3 surface is 77,844 H3 res-4 rows, 7.5 MB. I tested this from this machine on 2026-10-18 with DuckDB 1.5.5 over anonymous HTTPS against the v3 HbS cells.parquet. count(*) read only the footer and took 0.19 s. A filtered GROUP BY over 2 columns made 2 HEAD and 3 GET requests totalling about 0.8 MB, roughly 11% of the file, thanks to range requests. read_json on manifests/2026-10-18.json over HTTPS listed the 30 v3 surface keys. Polars 2.0.0 also worked: scan_parquet over https://, and over gs:// with skip_signature on a single key. P1 observation ingest already reads hive-partitioned Parquet with DuckDB (genomeos/observations/ingest.py), so this keeps continuity.
options.geo: DuckDB 1.5 has GEOMETRY as a built-in type (WKB-based). Its semantics are planar: plain ST_Distance returns degrees. Use ST_Distance_Sphere, ST_Distance_Spheroid or ST_DWithin_Spheroid for metres on WGS84. The spheroid functions expect [lat, lon] axis order, which is easy to get wrong. The spatial extension adds the ST_* functions and GDAL readers. H3 comes from the community extension h3 (Apache-2.0, maintainer isaacbrodsky, H3 core 4.5.0): h3_latlng_to_cell, h3_cell_to_parent, h3_grid_disk, h3_polygon_wkt_to_cells and others. I verified it: INSTALL h3 FROM community worked, and rolling the 77,844 res-4 cells up to res 2 gave 2,332 parents. Our h3_index strings work directly. A spatial join, for example an observation disc (lat, lon, radius_km) against cells, runs client-side as h3_grid_disk or a spheroid DWithin. GeoParquet is at 2.0.0-rc.1 (OGC incubating) and adds native Parquet geometry types. BigQuery loads GeoParquet columns as GEOGRAPHY, so the same files stay portable.
options.cost: The publisher pays every byte served. Cloud Storage internet egress is $0.12/GiB (0-10 TiB, worldwide excluding Asia and Australia), and Class B operations (GETs) are $0.0004 per 1,000. Always Free, aggregated over us-east1, us-central1 and us-west1, gives per month: 100 GB of egress from North America, 50,000 Class B operations and 5 GB-months of Standard storage. Storing the 0.27 GB release costs well under $0.01 a month (data-store design §9.2: about $0.03 per full download, about $30 per 1,000). Idle cost is $0. Range reads cut egress for selective queries (about 0.8 MB of 7.5 MB in the test). The querier pays nothing. The $300 kill switch (150% of budget) is therefore the backstop: it makes this bucket private. Requester Pays would bill readers instead, but it breaks credential-free reads (design §9.2), so it is not an option.
options.publicAccess: Anyone, with no account: SELECT ... FROM 'https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/releases/<release>/<path>'. Open CORS on the bucket (design C3) also lets DuckDB-WASM and Observable read it in a browser. Readers need exact keys, which they get from manifests/<release>.json, because anonymous users cannot list the bucket (legacyObjectReader).
options.ops: Nothing new to run beyond the existing publish and anonymous --verify-remote. Optional improvements: write surfaces and observations as GeoParquet; sort by (variant_id, h3_index) so row-group statistics prune well; consider a long-format table across variants split into one file per variant. Each new file type needs an entry in the manifest's closed media-type table.
options.limits: There is no listing, so globs fail. I verified this: DuckDB refuses '*' in HTTP paths ('Globs (*) for generic HTTP file is are not supported'). A gs:// glob needs ListObjectsV2 and returns 403 anonymously, and a Polars gs:// glob failed on the list request too. DuckDB table functions cannot take subqueries ('Table function cannot contain subqueries'), so a manifest-driven read takes two steps unless a catalog file is published (next option). The web bucket's objects are gzip Content-Encoding, and Cloud Storage decompressive transcoding silently ignores Range headers, so SQL against them downloads whole objects. Use the raw-bytes data store for SQL. There is no server-side compute: large joins pull data to the client. When the kill switch fires, all reads fail.

options.name: Read-only catalog file over the same Parquet: a view-only DuckDB database or a Frozen DuckLake
options.kind: Catalog layer that works on any cloud: one small metadata file per release, with no data copy and no server.
options.fit: This is the 'principled structure' with no standing resource. Each release gets a releases/<release>/atlas.duckdb that holds only views over explicit HTTPS keys taken from the manifest: observations, surfaces, registry and validation as separate relations, so the observation/surface split is visible in the schema. The file is itself a manifest object, sha256-pinned and immutable, and older releases stay attachable, so versioning is free. Users run ATTACH 'https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/releases/<r>/atlas.duckdb' and see named, typed tables. This fixes both the no-listing and the no-subquery problems above. DuckDB says such a file 'stays a few hundred kilobytes no matter how large the data it describes'. A Frozen DuckLake (DuckLake 1.0, April 2026) adds typed tables, snapshots, time travel and file-level statistics. ducklake_add_data_files registers existing Parquet files by reading only their metadata, which suits write-once buckets.
options.geo: Whatever DuckDB offers: built-in GEOMETRY, the spatial extension and the h3 community extension. Views can expose ST_Point(lon, lat) and keep radius_km explicit, never folded into a geometry.
options.cost: The same as the direct Parquet option, plus a few hundred KB per attach. Idle cost is $0. The publisher pays egress, and queriers pay nothing.
options.publicAccess: Anyone with no account, through DuckDB (CLI, Python, R, WASM). Other tools, such as Polars or pandas, read the same Parquet keys directly.
options.ops: One extra deterministic build step in build_data_release.py or promote.yml. Add .duckdb (and .ducklake) to the closed media-type table. Pin the DuckDB storage version, and test that old catalog files still attach.
options.limits: DuckDB-specific. Attaching over HTTPS or S3 is read-only by design. With DuckLake, the persisted DATA_PATH cannot be changed after creation (a documented, known limitation), so the public base URL must be final first. The catalog-file approach is new (a DuckDB blog post of 2026-10-07), so expect some churn.

options.name: BigQuery native (loaded) tables in a public dataset
options.kind: Serverless columnar data warehouse with managed storage.
options.fit: Strong for analytic SQL and the most familiar choice for others. Each release's Parquet is loaded into separate observations, surfaces, registry and validation tables, which keeps the invariant. Two ways to version: partition by a release DATE column, or keep one table per release. A partition untouched for 90 days moves to the long-term rate, which suits append-only data. Use an explicit schema with INT64 ac and an, and validate with the existing pandera schemas before loading. BigQuery does not enforce immutability: anyone with write can mutate a table. Releases therefore have to be guarded by our pipeline, and the tables become a second copy that must be verified against the hash-pinned manifest, for example with row counts and a fingerprint aggregate. At this data size, the 10 MB minimum per table referenced dominates billing, and clustering helps little (Google says tables under 64 MB gain negligibly).
options.geo: Native GEOGRAPHY on the WGS84 spheroid, with ST_DWITHIN, ST_INTERSECTS, ST_CONTAINS, ST_COVERS, ST_BUFFER, ST_CLUSTERDBSCAN and ST_REGIONSTATS. Spatial joins benefit from clustering on a GEOGRAPHY column, which cannot be a partition column. The only built-in grid functions are S2 (S2_CELLIDFROMPOINT, S2_COVERINGCELLIDS). There are no built-in H3 functions. H3 comes from CARTO's Analytics Toolbox core (BSD-3-Clause), which serves H3_FROMGEOGPOINT, H3_POLYFILL, H3_TOPARENT, H3_KRING and others to all authenticated BigQuery users from the carto-os (US multi-region) and carto-os-eu projects. The catch: carto-os is US multi-region and our bucket is us-east1. Either load into a US multi-region dataset (a one-off cross-region load billed for network) or self-deploy CARTO core into our own project. Equality joins and filters on a STRING h3_index need no UDF. GeoParquet loads straight into GEOGRAPHY.
options.cost: On-demand queries cost $6.25/TiB after the first 1 TiB per month, which is free per billing account. Each query bills at least 10 MB per table referenced and 10 MB per query. Storage is about $0.023/GiB-month active logical ($0.000031507/GiB-hour) and about $0.016 long-term ($0.000021918/GiB-hour). Physical storage is about $0.040 active and $0.020 long-term. The first 10 GiB per month is free, so our ~0.27 GB costs $0. Batch loads from Cloud Storage are free on the shared slot pool, and cross-region loads are billed for network. Idle cost is $0. Public queries: 'Query charges are incurred by the billing account attached to the project where the query jobs are run', and storage is charged to the dataset's project. So the publisher pays storage only. The Storage Read API is free up to 300 TiB a month per billing account, billed to the reader.
options.publicAccess: Not anonymous. Grant dataset READER to the specialGroup allAuthenticatedUsers ('All Authenticated Users'). Every query needs a Google account and a Cloud project to run the job in. The BigQuery sandbox needs no credit card (10 GiB storage, 1 TiB of queries a month, and the reader's own tables expire after 60 days). There are two other routes. (a) BigQuery sharing (formerly Analytics Hub) public data exchange: listings are discoverable by allAuthenticatedUsers. A subscriber gets a linked dataset in their own project and pays for the queries, the publisher pays storage, and exchanges themselves cost nothing extra. (b) The Google Cloud Public Datasets Program: Google pays storage and hosts the data under bigquery-public-data, users pay only for queries (1 TB a month free), and there is no SLA. The only intake I found is the address bq-public-data@google.com.
options.ops: A dataset, an IAM grant, and a load step per release in promote.yml. The WIF publisher needs BigQuery data-edit and job rights, and the step needs a post-load verification against the manifest. The kill switch does not cover BigQuery, but the exposure is storage-only, and that is free at this size. No server to run.
options.limits: At most 10,000 partitions per table, 4,000 partitions modified per job, a single partitioning column and up to 4 clustering columns. A second copy of the truth that can drift. No anonymous HTTP access. Location coupling with the CARTO UDFs.

options.name: BigQuery external tables and BigLake tables over the existing Parquet on GCS
options.kind: BigQuery SQL that reads the files in place on Cloud Storage, with no copy.
options.fit: Good as an optional SQL front door that never duplicates the truth. Table definitions point at the same immutable, hash-pinned release keys, so a new release means a new table definition or a UNION ALL view. Plain external tables require the querier to hold permissions on both the table and the Cloud Storage files. Our public role is legacyObjectReader (read by key, no list), so wildcard URIs will not work for others. Each table must list explicit URIs generated from the manifest, up to 10,000 per table. BigLake tables use a Cloud resource connection whose service account reads the files ('access delegation'), so readers only need access to the table, and wildcards work. Metadata caching speeds up layouts with many files or hive partitions. Slower than native tables, but zero drift.
options.geo: The same GoogleSQL GEOGRAPHY functions, built at query time with ST_GEOGPOINT(lon, lat). H3 through CARTO, with a location catch: external data must be colocated with the dataset. Our bucket is us-east1, so the dataset must be us-east1 as well. A US multi-region dataset is colocated only with us-central1 (or dual-regions that include Iowa), and 'Queries from any other single region incur data transfer charges'. carto-os exists only in the US and EU multi-regions, so H3 UDFs here mean self-deploying CARTO core into a us-east1 dataset, which needs a project bucket for its JS libraries.
options.cost: The querier pays on-demand bytes processed ($6.25/TiB after 1 TiB a month free). There is no BigQuery storage charge, and the long-term discount does not apply to external data. Refreshing the BigLake metadata cache, manually or automatically, is billed as bytes processed to the project that owns the table, which is us; it is small at this size. Cloud Storage's default rule bills operations and network for a read to the resource's project unless the request names a billing project. So Class B operations ($0.0004 per 1,000) and any inter-region transfer from other people's BigQuery jobs probably land on our bill. I did not verify that for BigQuery-originated reads.
options.publicAccess: The same as BigQuery: dataset READER for allAuthenticatedUsers, and the querier needs a Google account and a project. Plain external tables also need object read on the bucket, which allUsers already has.
options.ops: A CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE ... OPTIONS(format='PARQUET', uris=[...]) per release, generated from the manifest. BigLake adds a connection resource and a grant for its service account. No load step and no copy to verify.
options.limits: 10,000 URIs and 10 million files per external table, 600 TB maximum. Wildcards need list permission on a plain external table. Slower than native. Partition pruning only with hive layouts. The colocation constraint, plus the carto-os location mismatch.

options.name: BigQuery Apache Iceberg managed tables (formerly BigLake tables for Apache Iceberg in BigQuery)
options.kind: Open-table-format lakehouse, managed by BigQuery, with data in a bucket you own.
options.fit: Poor fit for this repo. BigQuery writes, compacts, clusters and garbage-collects data files in your bucket, and it warns that 'modifying data files ... outside of BigQuery can cause query failure or data loss'. That contradicts the data store's create-only, never-delete uploads, its hash-pinned keys and its manifest-first verification, so it would need its own bucket. Batch loads only append, which does fit append-only data. Time travel exists, but data files are garbage-collected once the window expires. Other engines read the tables through exported metadata snapshots (EXPORT TABLE METADATA, scheduled), another moving part.
options.geo: GEOGRAPHY is not supported in Iceberg managed table schemas, nor are JSON, RANGE, INTERVAL or BIGNUMERIC. Coordinates would have to be stored as lat/lon or WKB bytes and cast at query time. H3 as for BigQuery (CARTO).
options.cost: Data sits in Cloud Storage and is charged in full, historical data included. Automatic storage optimization is billed in Data Compute Units. Queries are billed as BigQuery queries. Load and export operations such as EXPORT METADATA use Enterprise edition pay-as-you-go slots, unlike standard BigQuery tables, for which these are free.
options.publicAccess: The same as BigQuery: authenticated users only, querier pays. External Iceberg readers need access to the managed bucket and its metadata.
options.ops: The heaviest BigQuery option: a connection, a managed bucket, a schedule for metadata exports, and BigQuery as the only writer.
options.limits: Partitioning only on DATE, DATETIME or TIMESTAMP, with no partition evolution. No rename, copy, clone or snapshot. One concurrent mutating DML statement per table. No GEOGRAPHY. Iceberg metadata may lag data streamed through the Storage Write API by 90 minutes. The docs were last updated 2026-10-16.

options.name: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL + PostGIS
options.kind: Managed relational database on an always-on instance (OLTP).
options.fit: The relational model is attractive: database-level CHECK (ac <= an), NOT NULL on radius_km and sampling_design, and foreign keys from observations to the registry would make schema violations hard errors inside the database. Versioning would use release columns, and UPDATE and DELETE privileges could be revoked. But it is a standing server built for transactions, not analytics. It cannot serve the public without an API in front, and it conflicts with the refit design's anti-goal 'Compute that keeps running' and with its commitment to create 'no standing GCP resources'. The data (<1 GB) fits easily; that is not the problem.
options.geo: PostGIS is supported on every major version: 3.5.2 on PostgreSQL 13-17 and 3.6.0 on PostgreSQL 18, including postgis_raster and sfcgal. It offers the geography type, ST_DWithin in metres and GiST indexes. The H3 extension (h3-pg) is not on Cloud SQL's list of supported extensions, and only listed extensions are available. H3 would have to be stored as text or bigint, with parents precomputed offline.
options.cost: Shared-core: db-f1-micro $0.0105/hour (about $7.67 a month) and db-g1-small $0.035/hour (about $25.55 a month); shared-core is not covered by the SLA. Dedicated Enterprise: $0.0413 per vCPU-hour plus $0.007 per GiB-hour, so 1 vCPU with 3.75 GiB is about $49 a month. SSD storage is $0.000232877/GiB-hour, about $0.17/GiB-month. Internet egress is $0.19/GiB without Interconnect, and an idle IPv4 address is $0.01/hour. The publisher pays all of it, including every public query, because queries go through our API.
options.publicAccess: No anonymous SQL. The public would reach it through an API we run, such as the planned Cloud Run API, and we would pay for that.
options.ops: Instance sizing, maintenance windows, backups, connection management, a public API, and a separate cost guard: the kill switch covers only the data-store bucket.
options.limits: Single primary with vertical scaling. Shared-core storage maximum 3,062 GiB. No SLA on shared-core. No h3 extension.

options.name: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
options.kind: Managed PostgreSQL-compatible database with Google's storage layer and a columnar engine.
options.fit: Overkill. It has the same server model and public-access problem as Cloud SQL, with a much higher price floor, and offers nothing this read-mostly, append-only, sub-GB dataset needs.
options.geo: PostGIS 3.6.0 and pgRouting are supported. No h3 extension is on the supported list.
options.cost: Default rates on the pricing page: $0.06608 per vCPU-hour and $0.0112 per GiB-hour. The smallest shape, c4a-highmem-1 (1 vCPU, 8 GB), is about $114 a month idle. The smallest N2, n2-highmem-2, is about $227 a month. Regional storage is $0.0004109/GiB-hour, about $0.30/GiB-month. A free trial cluster runs 30 days, up to 8 vCPUs and 1 TB. The publisher pays everything.
options.publicAccess: No anonymous access. It would need an API.
options.ops: Cluster and instance management, plus an API.
options.limits: The idle floor is more than half the $200 monthly budget. The same h3 gap as Cloud SQL.

options.name: Spanner
options.kind: Globally distributed relational database for transactions.
options.fit: No. It is built for high-throughput transactional writes at global scale. Our data is a small, batch, append-only corpus that is mostly read for analysis.
options.geo: The GoogleSQL data types reference lists no GEOGRAPHY type, and the PostgreSQL interface has no PostGIS. H3 could be stored only as INT64 or STRING, with no spatial functions.
options.cost: Standard edition is $0.90 per node-hour (Enterprise $1.23, Enterprise Plus $1.71). The smallest granular instance, 100 processing units, costs $0.09/hour, about $65.70 a month idle. Any provisioned capacity bills at least one hour. A free trial instance runs 90 days with 10 GiB.
options.publicAccess: No anonymous access. It would need an API.
options.ops: Instance and schema management, plus an API.
options.limits: No geospatial type. A standing cost for no benefit at this scale.

options.name: Firestore
options.kind: Serverless document database, billed per read and write.
options.fit: No. Billing is per document, and there are no SQL joins or aggregations over the corpus. One surface is 77,844 cells and there are 30 v3 surfaces, about 2.3 million documents. Reading a single full surface would use about 1.6 times the daily free read quota.
options.geo: No native geo queries. The documented workaround uses geohash ranges with client-side filtering of false positives ('These extra reads add cost and latency'). No H3.
options.cost: Free per day: 1 GiB stored, 50,000 document reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes, plus 10 GiB of egress a month. Beyond that, reads are $0.03 per 100,000 and writes $0.09 per 100,000. Public reads are billed to the publisher.
options.publicAccess: Security rules can allow unauthenticated reads through the SDKs and REST, but every read lands on our bill. The kill switch does not cover it, which makes it a scraping-cost risk.
options.ops: Data modelling into documents, security rules and index management.
options.limits: Not analytic. Geo queries are approximate. Costs scale with the number of documents read.

options.name: Bigtable
options.kind: Wide-column NoSQL store on provisioned nodes.
options.fit: No. It is built for very large, low-latency key-value workloads, and this corpus is under 1 GB of analytic tables.
options.geo: There is a 'Work with GEOGRAPHY data' guide for GoogleSQL for Bigtable, but that dialect has no JOIN, subqueries, UNION, CTEs, DML or DDL. Spatial joins would have to be designed into the row keys.
options.cost: Enterprise edition is $0.65 per node-hour (Enterprise Plus $0.85), billed 'even if your cluster is inactive'. One node is about $474.50 a month (Google's 30-day example: $468 for the node plus $8.50 for 50 GiB at $0.17/GiB). Data Boost is billed per SPU-second, with a 60 SPU-second minimum per request.
options.publicAccess: No anonymous access. It would need an API.
options.ops: Node provisioning, row-key design, plus an API.
options.limits: Its idle cost alone is more than double the monthly budget. Its SQL is too limited for analytics.

research: GCP options.notes:
BOTTOM LINE. For an open, append-only, versioned, mostly-read, geospatial corpus that today is 271 MB (248 objects; 266 MB of it in 62 Parquet files), the best structure is a file-based lake.

- **Keep the hash-pinned Parquet in the existing public data store as the only source of truth.** Move surfaces and observations to GeoParquet.
- **Publish a small read-only catalog file with each release.** This is a view-only DuckDB database, or later a Frozen DuckLake. It exposes separate observations, surfaces, registry and validation relations over the manifest's exact keys.
- **Readers need no account:** `ATTACH 'https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/releases/<r>/atlas.duckdb'`.
- **If a cloud SQL front door is wanted, add BigQuery as an optional mirror.** Use native tables loaded from those same files, in a public dataset (allAuthenticatedUsers, or a public listing in BigQuery sharing; later, possibly the Public Datasets Program).
  - The querier pays for queries. The publisher pays storage only, which is free under the 10 GiB tier.
  - Treat it as a derived copy, verified against the manifest, never as the truth.

**Always-on databases do not fit.** Cloud SQL (about $8 to $49+ a month), AlloyDB (about $114 to $227+), Spanner (about $66) and Bigtable (about $475) bill even when idle. They conflict with the refit design's anti-goals: "Compute that keeps running" and creating "no standing GCP resources". None of them carries an H3 extension. Firestore bills the publisher for every public read and cannot do analytics.

**The key distinction is who pays.**
- **Files on the public bucket:** anyone can query with no account, but the publisher pays egress ($0.12/GiB after 100 GB a month free from North America) and GET operations ($0.0004 per 1,000 after 50,000 free). The 150% kill switch is the backstop. Range reads keep selective queries cheap: a test read about 0.8 MB of a 7.5 MB surface.
- **BigQuery:** only signed-in Google users with a Cloud project can query (the sandbox needs no credit card), and they pay for their own queries. Google's docs say: "Query charges are incurred by the billing account attached to the project where the query jobs are run." The kill switch does not cover BigQuery, but the publisher's exposure there is storage only, and that is free at this size.
- **Requester Pays** would push bucket costs onto readers, but it breaks credential-free reads, as data-store design §9.2 already says.

**BigQuery gotchas for this repo.**
1. **No built-in H3**, only S2. H3 comes from CARTO's Analytics Toolbox core (BSD-3-Clause) in the public projects carto-os (US multi-region) and carto-os-eu.
2. **Location mismatch.** Our bucket is us-east1. A US multi-region dataset is colocated only with us-central1, so external or BigLake tables over our bucket must sit in a us-east1 dataset, where carto-os is unavailable. The alternatives are self-deploying CARTO core, or loading native tables into a US multi-region dataset (a one-off cross-region load billed for network). Joins and filters on a STRING h3_index need no UDF at all.
3. **Plain external tables cannot use wildcards** for other people. Our public role reads by key but cannot list, so each table must enumerate explicit URIs (up to 10,000), or use BigLake with a connection.
4. **Iceberg managed tables don't fit.** They do not support GEOGRAPHY, and BigQuery rewrites and garbage-collects files in the bucket. That contradicts the create-only, never-delete store.

**How the invariants map onto the lake design.**
- **Observations and surfaces:** separate files and separate catalog relations, never one table.
- **Counts, not frequencies:** ac and an stay integer columns, and no catalog view adds an ac/an column.
- **Hard errors on schema violations:** enforced at build time by the existing pandera schemas. In any SQL mirror, use an explicit schema and a zero-error load.
- **No inference on the serving path:** every option above only reads precomputed artifacts.
- **Missing extent or ascertainment:** radius_km and sampling_design stay explicit, required columns. They are never folded into a geometry or defaulted.

**What I verified empirically on 2026-10-18,** using anonymous HTTPS against the public data store only: no cloud commands, no credentials, about 1 to 2 MB of egress, and extensions installed into the scratchpad.
- **DuckDB 1.5.5 range reads:** count(*) read only the footer and took 0.19 s on the v3 HbS cells.parquet (77,844 rows). A 2-column filtered aggregate made 3 GETs totalling about 0.8 MB.
- **Globs fail without listing:**
  - DuckDB refuses `*` in HTTP paths.
  - An anonymous gs:// glob returns 403, because listing is denied.
  - DuckDB table functions cannot take a subquery. So a manifest-driven multi-file read takes two steps, unless a catalog file is published. That is the main practical argument for publishing one.
- **Manifest and extensions:** read_json over HTTPS on manifests/2026-10-18.json worked and listed the 30 v3 surfaces. The h3 extension (H3 4.5.0) installed, and the res-4 to res-2 rollup gave 2,332 parent cells. The spatial extension installed, and ST_Distance_Sphere worked.
- **Polars 2.0.0** scan_parquet worked over https:// and over gs:// with skip_signature on a single key. Its gs:// glob failed on the list request.
- **Web bucket:** its objects are gzip Content-Encoding. Cloud Storage silently ignores Range headers under decompressive transcoding, so it is unsuitable for SQL range reads. Only the raw-bytes data store is.

**Not verified.**
- Whether Cloud Storage operation charges caused by other people's BigQuery external or BigLake reads land on our project. Cloud Storage's general rule bills the resource's project unless the request names a billing project.
- Whether BigQuery datasets accept allUsers, as opposed to allAuthenticatedUsers. In practice it would not matter, because every query job needs a Cloud project.
- The intake process for the Public Datasets Program. The docs give only the address bq-public-data@google.com.
- The exact current Cloud Storage at-rest price. I relied on design §9.2's "well under $0.01 a month" for the 0.27 GB release.

**Repo context.**
- I read AGENTS.md, docs/data-store.md, docs/cost-controls.md, the data-store design (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-17-data-store-on-gcs-design.md), the refit design, and genomeos/observations/schema.py and ingest.py. ingest.py already uses DuckDB over hive-partitioned Parquet, and `read = [duckdb, h3]` is already an optional dependency group.
- The refit design is not on main. It is on origin/docs/automated-refit-design at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-17-automated-refit-pipeline-design.md.
- The scratchpad test scripts are <scratchpad>/duck_test.py, duck_test2.py and polars_test.py.

design: integrity.title: Integrity and growth first: keep hash-pinned Parquet on the public data store as the only truth, and add a typed, per-release table catalog over it (no database)
design: integrity.recommendation:
Don't add a database. Keep the immutable, sha256-pinned Parquet files in the public data store (https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/) as the only source of truth. Give them a principled structure in four parts.

(1) Logical tables with frozen contracts. Each kind of data becomes a named table with a frozen contract, and every file is physically separated by key prefix: measured/ (allele and carrier observations, as two separate tables), inferred/ (surfaces, later burden), reference/ (P0 populations, aliases, the variant registry), evidence/ (validation) and meta/ (manifests, sources and terms, withdrawals, the served pin). Observations and surfaces then cannot share a table, a key or a prefix.

(2) Partition keys in the path. Partition values go in key=value path segments, so a reader can prune files from the manifest's explicit URL list without listing the bucket. Each value is also stored as a column inside the file, so files describe themselves.

(3) A catalog per release. Each release gets a deterministic text catalog, releases/<r>/catalog.sql: CREATE VIEW statements over exact manifest URLs, organised into schemas measured, inferred, reference, evidence and meta. It is reviewed by diff in git and pinned in the manifest. A convenience atlas.duckdb built from it can be opened with ATTACH and needs no account.

(4) A derived index for location queries. A cell-major cross-surface index, partitioned by H3 res-1 parent and covering the served set, answers "this cell across all surfaces". It is a rebuildable derived object with recorded lineage, never truth.

Fitting moves to the published observation table by file sha256 (this closes refit 'gap 3'). Each artifact records its exact input files. Nothing on the serving path computes science.

What I measured on 2026-10-18, locally only: copies of the 31 local res-4 surfaces served by a local HTTP server that supports range requests, with the bytes served logged; no GCS. In today's layout (one row group per file, string h3), a point query across the 31 surfaces cost 124 requests and 40.0 MB. With the same 14 columns but 8,192-row groups it cost 3.8 MB. With a UBIGINT h3 column and zstd it cost 2.6 MB. The cell-major index (458 res-1 partitions, 148.6 MB in total) answered it in 7 requests and 85.6 KB. Hive pruning works on an explicit URL list: a deliberately missing, non-matching URL in the list was never fetched. Through an attached catalog, an observation disc query on the 994-row HbS parity parquet took 15 requests and 845 KB. The catalog builder reads every file footer when it creates the views, so a missing or renamed key fails the build. The .duckdb file is not byte-deterministic (two builds differed in 2 bytes), which is why catalog.sql, not the .duckdb file, is canonical.

BigQuery stays out for now. If an authenticated SQL front door is ever wanted, use external tables over the same hash-pinned keys (no copy, so no drift), not loaded tables.
design: integrity.layout:
Bucket and key rule unchanged: releases/<release>/<path>, an unchanged file reuses its earlier key, create-only, raw bytes, sha256 in the manifest. New paths, added beside today's:

releases/<r>/tables/measured/allele_observations/v1/source=<source>/ingest_version=<iv>/locus=<bucket>/part-0.parquet
  locus = chr1..chr22|chrX|chrY|chrM for chr-pos-ref-alt; otherwise the namespace (hla, kir, mic, phenotype). This generalises ingest.py's chrom=, which today yields chrom=phenotype%3Ag6pd. Files are sorted by (variant_id, population_id, source_record_id), with row groups of about 64K rows, so min/max statistics on variant_id prune.
releases/<r>/tables/measured/carrier_observations/v1/source=<s>/ingest_version=<iv>/part-0.parquet   (carriers/n_individuals; never unioned with ac/an)
releases/<r>/tables/reference/populations/v1/registry_version=<RELEASE+sha256.DIGEST>/{populations,population_aliases}.parquet
releases/<r>/tables/reference/variants/v1/registry_version=<curated-v1-candidate.N>/variants.parquet   (from curated_variants.tsv and variant_normalization.tsv)
releases/<r>/store/artifacts/<variant>__<model>__<data>/{cells.parquet,manifest.json}   (the 61 legacy artifacts; keys unchanged)
releases/<r>/tables/inferred/surface_cells/v3/entity=<slug>/model_version=<m>/data_version=<d>/h3_res=<k>/cells.parquet   (new artifacts. The slug is the existing ':'-to-'__' form, so no percent-encoding appears in URLs. String h3_index is kept, plus parent columns, sorted by h3_index, 8,192-row groups.)
releases/<r>/tables/inferred/cells_by_location/<served_epoch>/h3_r1=<hex>/part-0.parquet   (derived. Rows of every served surface, sorted by (h3_cell, variant_id, model_version, data_version). Rebuilt only when the served pin changes; old epochs are never deleted.)
releases/<r>/tables/evidence/{crossval,refit_qc,parity}/...   (today's validation/ files stay where they are; the catalog adds views over them)
releases/<r>/tables/meta/{objects,sources,artifacts,artifact_inputs,withdrawn,served}.parquet   (flattened from data/releases/*.json, WITHDRAWN.json and served.json, so meta is queryable rather than JSON-only)
releases/<r>/catalog.sql   (canonical; also committed to git) and releases/<r>/atlas.duckdb   (a convenience build of catalog.sql, pinned by sha256)
manifests/<r>.json   (unchanged: the root of trust that lists everything above)

Formats: Parquet with zstd for new tables (snappy stays valid for legacy artifacts). Every file carries key-value metadata: genomeos.table, genomeos.schema_version (MAJOR.MINOR), genomeos.contract_sha256, and the producing git SHA. Media-type table: add .sql (application/sql) and .duckdb (application/vnd.duckdb), deliberately. The web bucket keeps its GOSA and JSON keys. Its observations JSON becomes a projection generated from measured.allele_observations and checked by digest, never a second source.
design: integrity.schemas:
Contracts live in contract/tables/<table>.v<MAJOR>.schema.json, frozen from the pandera schemas as freeze_contract.py already does. MINOR changes are additive and appear only in new files. MAJOR means a new table directory (/v2/), with the old one still listed. NULL is never used as a default: every view exposes schema_version, so a reader can tell 'not in this format' from a value.

measured.allele_observations. PK (ingest_version, source_record_id). Columns: variant_id, rsid (nullable), population_id, lat, lon, radius_km > 0, ac INT64 >= 0, an INT64 > 0, source, assay, date_lower and date_upper INT64 (years BP), sampling_design (enum of 7), disease_ascertainment_excluded BOOLEAN NOT NULL, cohort_id, ingest_version, registry_version, plus citation_id (FK meta.sources). Checks: ac <= an, date_lower <= date_upper. No view computes ac/an. Join key to the registry: (registry_version, population_id).

measured.carrier_observations. The same columns, with carriers and n_individuals in place of ac and an. A separate table; never unioned with allele_observations.

reference.populations. PK (registry_version, population_id). Columns: lat, lon, uncertainty_radius_km > 0 (no default), location_type, provenance, biocultural_notice (nullable).

reference.population_aliases. Unique (registry_version, source, label), mapping to population_id. The legacy labels 'afnd-2026-08' and 'map-survey-coordinates-v1' get explicit legacy registry_version rows; old surfaces are not rewritten.

reference.variants. PK (registry_version, variant_id). Columns: gene, namespace, rsid, inheritance, observation_type, review status, publication_eligible.

inferred.surface_cells. PK (variant_id, model_version, data_version, h3_res, h3_index). Columns: post_median, post_mean, post_sd, q025, q975, q25, q75, support, posterior_contraction, dist_nearest_obs_km, h3_parent_r0..r3, artifact_format. Format 3 adds the §6 columns as required: eff_n_in_range, expected_alt_count, beta_design_applied, de_novo_dominated, registry_version.

inferred.cells_by_location. The same key, plus h3_r1 and h3_cell UBIGINT; covers the served epoch only.

meta.artifacts. PK (variant_id, model_version, data_version). Columns: first_release, cells_key, cells_sha256, manifest_sha256, grid_sha256, n_cells, n_observations, served (bool, from the pin), withdrawn (bool).

meta.artifact_inputs. PK (artifact PK, input_table, input_key). Columns: input_sha256, ingest_version, registry_version, inputs_hash, fit_config_sha256, seed, git_sha. This is the only link from a surface to its observations, so the two are joined, never merged.

meta.objects. PK (release, path). Columns: key, bytes, sha256, media_type, in_git, sources[].

meta.sources. PK source_id. Columns: terms_status, non_commercial, checked_at, citation.

meta.withdrawn. PK key.
queries: Observations of V within 500 km of (lat, lon), using the disc and not only the centre. A reader runs ATTACH 'https://storage.googleapis.com/genomeos-atlas-data/releases/<r>/atlas.duckdb' AS atlas (READ_ONLY); LOAD spatial; then: SELECT o.cohort_id, o.sampling_design, o.assay, o.ac, o.an, o.radius_km, s.citation, ST_Distance_Sphere(ST_Point(o.lon,o.lat), ST_Point(:lon,:lat))/1000 AS centre_km FROM atlas.measured.allele_observations o JOIN atlas.meta.sources s ON s.source_id=o.source WHERE o.locus='chr11' AND o.variant_id=:v AND o.lat BETWEEN :lat-9.5 AND :lat+9.5 AND ST_Distance_Sphere(ST_Point(o.lon,o.lat), ST_Point(:lon,:lat))/1000 - o.radius_km <= 500. The locus filter prunes to one partition per (source, ingest_version) from the path alone. Row-group min/max on variant_id skips other variants, and the latitude box is a cheap prefilter before the spherical test. Measured locally on the 994-row HbS parity parquet through an attached catalog: 15 HTTP requests, 845 KB, 39 rows within 500 km of Lagos. ac and an come back as counts, and no frequency column exists to return.

The value of every surface at one point, across all variants and versions, including res-3 v1/v2. Compute c4 = h3_latlng_to_cell(lat, lon, 4), c3 = h3_cell_to_parent(c4, 3) and r1 = h3_cell_to_parent(c4, 1). Served surfaces: SELECT variant_id, model_version, data_version, post_median, q025, q975, support, posterior_contraction, dist_nearest_obs_km FROM atlas.inferred.cells_by_location WHERE h3_r1 = :r1 AND h3_cell = :c4. Superseded versions: UNION ALL the same columns FROM atlas.inferred.surface_cells WHERE (h3_res = 4 AND h3_index = :c4_hex) OR (h3_res = 3 AND h3_index = :c3_hex). Join meta.artifacts to flag served and withdrawn rows. Measured locally for the 31 res-4 surfaces: the cell index took 7 requests and 85.6 KB. Today's per-artifact layout (one row group per file) took 124 requests and 40.0 MB, and the same columns with 8,192-row groups took 3.8 MB. Mapping one cell across all 61 local artifacts (res 3 and res 4) returned 61 rows in 0.03 s from local files.

Observation diff between two data_versions of a dataset (refit review), keyed by source identity. WITH a AS (SELECT input_key FROM atlas.meta.artifact_inputs WHERE data_version=:old AND input_table='allele_observations'), b AS (... :new ...). Then FULL OUTER JOIN the two observation sets on source_record_id, where each set is read from the files its artifact_inputs rows name, through the partition paths (source=, ingest_version=). Classify each row as added, removed, or changed (any of ac, an, radius_km, sampling_design, cohort_id or population_id differs), and GROUP BY source, sampling_design, cohort_id. Because each artifact pins its exact input files by sha256, the diff is between byte-identified inputs and not between two rebuilds that might differ. The same meta tables answer the release diff (a FULL OUTER JOIN of meta.objects on path for R1 against R2, comparing sha256 and key) and the refit selection rule (EXISTS in meta.artifacts across all releases).
design: integrity.cost:
Assumptions: Cloud Storage Standard in us-east1 at about $0.020/GB-month (an assumption, not re-verified today). Internet egress $0.12/GiB after the Always Free 100 GB a month from North America. Class B operations $0.0004 per 1,000 after 50,000 free. No standing compute, so the idle cost is $0. Byte figures come from the local measurements above.

NOW. The 0.27 GB release, plus about 0.15 GB for a cell index and well under 0.01 GB for observation, registry and meta tables, is about 0.45 GB, about $0.01 a month. Usage scenario: 100 full downloads (27 GB) plus 10,000 SQL queries averaging 1 MB (10 GB) is 37 GB, inside the 100 GB free tier, so about $0 a month. Even at 400 full downloads a month, egress is about $1 a month.

AT 100x (about 3,000 surface versions, or the 698 curated variants with about 4 versions each; observations at curated scale of about 10M rows). Surfaces truth: about 3,000 x 6 MB = 18 GB. One cell index per served epoch: 54M rows at about 62 B/row is about 3.3 GB, times about 20 epochs over the period is about 66 GB. Observations: about 0.5 GB. Total about 85 GB of storage, about $1.70 a month. If 500-draw matrices are published (about 311 MB each uncompressed, 698 variants), add about 217 GB, about $4.30 a month.

Egress dominates at 100x. A full-release download becomes about 20 GB (about $2.40 each). The scenario of 50 full downloads (1,000 GB), 50,000 queries at about 1 MB (50 GB) and 100,000 GETs gives (1,050 - 100 free) GB x $0.12 = about $114, plus about $0.02 for operations. That totals about $116 a month, under the $200 budget. The kill switch at $300 is the backstop, and it also takes down the catalog and every query.

Levers that keep it bounded: fetch_data.py --prefix by table and partition so nobody needs the full tree; the HF mirror for bulk snapshots; and the cell index, which cuts point-query egress about 470x compared with today's layout.

Literal whole-genome upper bound (about 1.2e10 observation rows at an estimated 25 to 40 B/row): 300 to 500 GB in the same layout, about $6 to $10 a month for storage. It is feasible without a redesign, but mirroring gnomAD wholesale is not recommended.
migration: 1. Freeze per-table contracts: generate contract/tables/{allele_observations,carrier_observations,populations,population_aliases,variants,surface_cells}.v1.schema.json from the existing pandera schemas, using freeze_contract.py's pattern. Every writer stamps genomeos.table, schema_version and contract_sha256 into the Parquet key-value metadata. The catalog builder refuses a file whose metadata or columns do not match its contract (a hard error, §12).

2. Publish the measured tables. Extend genomeos/observations/ingest.py to write source=/ingest_version=/locus= partitions (replacing chrom-only partitioning, which mis-buckets the hla:, kir: and phenotype: namespaces). Validate on write as it does today. Make (ingest_version, source_record_id) the key, and keep carrier rows in their own table. Publish the first ingest_versions for map, afnd, wbbc and gnomad_hgdp_1kg through build_data_release.py, adding the media types deliberately.

3. Publish a P0 registry release (populations and aliases with the RELEASE+sha256 identity) under tables/reference/. Map the legacy labels 'afnd-2026-08' and 'map-survey-coordinates-v1' to explicit legacy registry_version rows instead of rewriting any served surface. Add population_id and registry_version to the observations so the registry join is exact rather than falling back to population_label or cohort_id.

4. Close refit gap 3: fits read observations from the published table files by sha256, and every artifact writes meta.artifact_inputs rows (input keys and sha256s, registry_version, grid sha256, FitConfig hash, seed, git SHA). The web observations JSON becomes a projection exported from the table, checked by digest, and gains population_id, rsid, source and date fields as a web-format MINOR change.

5. Change the artifact writer, for new artifacts only. Format 2.1 changes only the physical layout: 8,192-row groups, sorted string h3_index, and h3_parent_r0..r3 columns. Format 3 adds the missing §6 columns as required. New artifacts publish under tables/inferred/surface_cells/v3/entity=/model_version=/data_version=/h3_res=. The 61 legacy artifacts keep their keys and are listed in the catalog as-is. Optionally, they can be re-listed byte-identically at hive paths, for about 0.23 GB more storage.

6. Add catalog generation to build_data_release.py, or to the refit stage job. It flattens manifests, sources, WITHDRAWN.json and the served pin into tables/meta/*.parquet, builds the served-epoch cells_by_location index, writes the deterministic catalog.sql (commits it, then diffs it in review) and builds atlas.duckdb from it. It verifies that every view binds, that path partition values equal the in-file min and max, that row counts and sha256s match the manifest, and that no file appears under both the measured/ and inferred/ prefixes. Both catalog files are added to the manifest last.

7. Leave the readers alone: fetch_data.py stays standard-library only, because catalog files are ordinary keyed objects. Document three read paths in docs/data-store.md: ATTACH the .duckdb file; run catalog.sql in any DuckDB; or read the Parquet keys directly with pandas, Polars or Arrow. Point the P4 API at the same catalog (DuckDB over the same keys) so it gets no private schema.

8. Defer, and decide on demand: Frozen DuckLake as an alternative catalog over the same files (file-level statistics, snapshots) once the layout settles; BigQuery external tables over the same keys only if authenticated cross-join users appear. Neither moves or copies data.
risks: Small files at 100x. Thousands of per-artifact files mean a footer read for each file a query touches. Mitigation: hive pruning on the path keys (verified to skip files that do not match), 8,192-row groups (10x less egress than today in the test), and the cell-major index for cross-surface queries. The residual cost is the 61 legacy artifacts, which have no key=value paths and cannot be pruned.

Catalog determinism. A .duckdb file is not byte-deterministic (two builds differed in 2 bytes), which conflicts with the deterministic-build rule if it is treated as truth. Mitigation: catalog.sql is canonical and diffed in git; the .duckdb is a pinned convenience copy, and CI checks that its view definitions equal catalog.sql.

Engine lock-in and churn. The view-only DuckDB catalog mode is new (a blog post of 2026-10-07), and storage versions change. Mitigation: everything underneath is plain Parquet with documented paths, any engine can read it, and CI pins the DuckDB storage version and tests that older catalogs still attach.

Schema evolution can look like defaults. union_by_name fills older files with NULL for newer columns, which a reader could mistake for a value. Mitigation: views expose schema_version and artifact_format, never union across a MAJOR, and any new required ascertainment field means a new table MAJOR and re-ingest, not a backfill.
Partition keys drift from contents. A path value can disagree with the in-file column. Mitigation: a build-time check that each file's min and max equal its path value, and a hard error otherwise.

Derived index mistaken for truth. Mitigation: cells_by_location lives under its own prefix with an epoch, records its lineage (the input artifact keys and sha256s in meta), and is rebuilt only from published artifacts. The API and QC may use it, but citation and reproduction always resolve to per-artifact files.

Egress at 100x comes mainly from bulk downloads. When the kill switch fires, every read fails, including the catalog, so SQL users see an outage, not a slowdown. Mitigation: prefix-level fetches, the HF mirror for bulk snapshots, and per-table manifests so users download what they need.

Manifest growth. Each release lists the full logical tree, which grows with every version; at 100x, expect over 10,000 objects and a multi-MB manifest. Mitigation: per-table sub-manifests, each hash-pinned from the release manifest, so trust stays rooted in one file.

Observation identity. Diffs and reproduction depend on source_record_id staying stable across ingest_versions. An adapter that re-derives ids differently would make every row look new. Mitigation: a contract test per adapter that re-ingesting the same raw input yields identical ids.

Takedown and caching. The docs conflict on Cache-Control (3600 s versus one year). Catalogs and index files inherit whichever value applies, so a withdrawn key can keep being served from caches. Resolve this before publishing catalogs, and have the catalog builder refuse withdrawn keys.

Scope creep toward a wholesale gnomAD mirror. The layout scales to it, but it would turn the observations table into a copy of upstream rather than harmonised, ascertainment-labelled evidence. Keep the table at fitted and curated scope unless the owner decides otherwise.
whyNotOthers: BigQuery native (loaded) tables: a second, mutable copy of the truth. Anyone with write access can change it, so every release would need re-verifying against the manifest. Every query needs a Google account and a Cloud project, which breaks the no-account principle. There are no built-in H3 functions, and the CARTO toolbox is US/EU multi-region while the bucket is in us-east1. At this size the 10 MB minimum billed per table referenced dominates, and clustering gains little.

BigQuery external or BigLake tables over the same keys: no copy, so no drift, and the best later option if authenticated SQL users appear. Not now: they need accounts, a plain external table is limited to 10,000 explicit URIs (it cannot use wildcards without list permission), the dataset must be colocated in us-east1, and BigLake adds a connection resource and metadata-refresh billing to the project.

BigQuery Iceberg managed tables: BigQuery rewrites, compacts and garbage-collects data files in the bucket, which contradicts the create-only, never-delete, hash-pinned store. They do not support GEOGRAPHY, and they partition only on dates.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL + PostGIS: database CHECK and foreign-key constraints are attractive, but pandera validation on write plus the catalog-build checks give the same hard errors without a server. It is a standing resource (about $8 to $49+ a month), which conflicts with the refit design's 'no standing GCP resources'. It cannot serve the public without an API we run and pay for, it has no h3 extension, and every query lands on our bill outside the kill switch.
AlloyDB: the same model as Cloud SQL, with an idle floor of about $114 to $227 a month, more than half the budget, for a read-mostly, sub-GB corpus.
Spanner: built for globally distributed transactional writes. It has no geography type, and its smallest instance idles at about $66 a month.
Firestore: billed per document read, with no joins or aggregation. A single surface is 77,844 documents, and public reads land on our bill outside the kill switch.
Bigtable: about $475 a month for one node, billed even when idle; its SQL has no joins. Built for a key-value workload this corpus does not have.

Frozen DuckLake as the catalog today: a good fit later, with typed tables, snapshots and file-level statistics over existing files, and it adopts the same Parquet without moving it. Deferred, not rejected: it is new, its DATA_PATH cannot change after creation, and the plain-text catalog.sql is deterministic, diffable and enough at today's scale.

Files with no catalog (the status quo): integrity is already strong, but readers must hand-assemble URL lists, because the bucket cannot be listed and DuckDB table functions cannot take subqueries. Nothing marks which files are measured and which are inferred, and the per-artifact layout cost 40 MB for a point query across only 31 surfaces.

design: cost.title: Keep files on GCS as the only source of truth; add a published catalog file and partition-pruned derived tables. No database.
design: cost.recommendation:
Do not adopt a database. Keep the hash-pinned, immutable, manifest-driven files in `genomeos-atlas-data` as the single source of truth, and spend the effort on two cheap additions instead: (a) **derived, partition-pruned Parquet tables** published beside the per-artifact directories, and (b) a **tiny read-only DuckDB catalog file per release** that names their exact keys, so readers get typed tables with no account, no listing and no server.

This is the only option whose idle cost is $0, whose reader cost is $0, and which needs no identity, no instance and no second copy of the truth. Every always-on option bills before anyone queries: Cloud SQL ~$8-49/mo, AlloyDB ~$114+, Spanner ~$66, Bigtable ~$475 — the last three consume or exceed the whole $200 budget doing nothing, and none can serve the public without an API we also pay for and operate. They also fail the refit design's anti-goals ("compute that keeps running", "this pipeline creates no standing GCP resources").

The real finding is that today's file *layout*, not the file *approach*, is what will break as the corpus grows. Each `cells.parquet` is a single row group of 77,844 rows, so Parquet statistics prune nothing. Measured over anonymous HTTPS with DuckDB 1.5.5: a one-cell lookup in one v3 surface cost 1 HEAD + 5 GET = **2.85 MB** (38% of the 7.5 MB file). The same answer across all 30 served surfaces would be ~85 MB of egress for a 60-byte result. After re-encoding into a cell-major table hive-partitioned by H3 res-0 parent (93 non-empty partitions, max 4.5 MB, median 1.2 MB), the identical 30-variant point query read **1,713 B of partition metadata + 859,459 B from the one relevant partition**, opening 2 of 93 files. That is a ~100x egress reduction on the most expensive likely query, and it is what keeps a file-based design inside the budget at 100x traffic. The re-encode also shrinks bytes: the 30 v3 surfaces are 225 MB as published and 147 MB as one zstd cell-major table (-35%); one surface re-encoded at ROW_GROUP_SIZE 8192 + zstd is 5.3 MB vs 7.5 MB (-29%).

The catalog file solves the two mechanical blockers confirmed by test: anonymous readers cannot list the bucket (globs fail — DuckDB refuses `*` in HTTP paths, an anonymous `gs://` glob gets 403), and DuckDB table functions cannot take subqueries (so a manifest-driven read cannot be one statement). A view-only `.duckdb` holding views over the 30 explicit HTTPS keys built to **274 KB** and attaches read-only. Readers then type `ATTACH '…/releases/<r>/atlas.duckdb' (READ_ONLY); SELECT … FROM atlas.surfaces.cells WHERE …` and get pruning for free.

If a cloud SQL front door is ever wanted, add BigQuery **native** tables later as an explicitly derived mirror (querier pays; publisher pays storage only, free under 10 GiB). Strictly optional, never the truth.
design: cost.layout:
Everything stays under the existing release prefix `releases/<release>/`, create-only, sha256-pinned in `data/releases/<release>.json`. Nothing existing moves or changes meaning.

KEEP AS-IS (citable units, unchanged keys):
```
releases/<r>/store/artifacts/<variant>__<model>__<data>/cells.parquet   # the citable artifact
releases/<r>/store/artifacts/<variant>__<model>__<data>/manifest.json
releases/<r>/validation/**, registry/**, raw/**, sources/**
manifests/<r>.json
```

ADD (derived tables; one logical table = one hive-partitioned directory):
```
releases/<r>/tables/surface_cells/res=4/h3_r0=<res0 cell>/part-0.parquet
releases/<r>/tables/surface_cells/res=3/h3_r0=<res0 cell>/part-0.parquet
releases/<r>/tables/observations/entity=<chr11|hla|kir|cyt|mic|phenotype>/part-0.parquet
releases/<r>/tables/carrier_observations/entity=kir/part-0.parquet
releases/<r>/tables/populations/part-0.parquet
releases/<r>/tables/population_aliases/part-0.parquet
releases/<r>/tables/artifacts/part-0.parquet          # one row per (variant, model, data) version
releases/<r>/tables/release_objects/part-0.parquet    # every object of every release, for manifest diffs
releases/<r>/tables/grid_cells/res=4/h3_r0=…/part-0.parquet   # H3 cell -> lat, lon, worldpop_pop
releases/<r>/tables/validation_qc/part-0.parquet
releases/<r>/atlas.duckdb                             # ~270 KB read-only catalog, views only
```

FORMATS AND ENCODING RULES (the load-bearing part):
- Parquet with **zstd**, not snappy: -29% on a surface at equal speed, and egress is the bill.
- **ROW_GROUP_SIZE 8192-30720; never one row group per file.** This single change is what makes HTTP range reads work; today's one-row-group files defeat statistics entirely.
- Sort order is the access order: `surface_cells` by `(h3_index, variant_id)` (cell-major, because the cross-variant point read is the expensive one); `observations` by `(variant_id, population_id)`.
- Partition key `h3_r0` = the H3 resolution-0 parent, a prefix of the index, free to compute and stable forever (93 non-empty partitions for the current global population-positive grid). `res` is a separate partition level so the res-3 (v1/v2) and res-4 (v3) grids never share a file.
- Keep `h3_index` as the published string (compatibility with today's artifacts and the web GOSA objects) and add `h3` UBIGINT plus `h3_r0`. The string column is ~0.5 MB of a 7.5 MB file; the nine double columns are 778 KB each, so they, not the key, dominate.
- GeoParquet is optional and off the critical path. Coordinates stay explicit `lat`, `lon`, `radius_km` / `uncertainty_radius_km` columns, never folded into a geometry — the extent must stay separately visible (§6).
- Target 1-50 MB per file; stay under ~150 MB to avoid composite uploads (no md5).
- Keep the per-artifact `cells.parquet` forever. The derived table is a deterministic re-encoding of the same facts; the artifact remains what a citation resolves to.
design: cost.schemas:
Seven core tables plus bookkeeping. Observations and surfaces are separate tables with separate provenance; allele counts and carrier counts are separate tables (§4, §7.1b). No view anywhere computes `ac/an`.

**surface_cells** (inferred). PK `(h3_index, res, variant_id, model_version, data_version)`; partitions `res`, `h3_r0`. Today's 14 columns (`h3_index`, `variant_id`, `post_median`, `post_mean`, `post_sd`, `q025`, `q975`, `q25`, `q75`, `support`, `posterior_contraction`, `dist_nearest_obs_km`, `model_version`, `data_version`) plus `h3` UBIGINT, `h3_r0`, `res`, `registry_version`, and the design §6 columns as they land (`eff_n_in_range`, `expected_alt_count`, `beta_design_applied`, `de_novo_dominated`). `support` keeps the enum `observed|interpolated|prior_dominated|unknown`; every aggregate filters on it and returns the excluded fraction.

**observations** (measured). PK `source_record_id` (`namespace:sha256`, already unique); partition `entity`, derived from the variant namespace because chromosome alone does not cover `hla:`/`kir:`/`cyt:`/`mic:`/`phenotype:` (`ingest.py` already encodes this as `chrom=phenotype%3Ag6pd`). Columns: the 17 of `OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA` verbatim (`variant_id`, `rsid`, `population_id`, `lat`, `lon`, `radius_km`, `ac` Int64, `an` Int64, `source_record_id`, `source`, `assay`, `date_lower`, `date_upper`, `sampling_design`, `disease_ascertainment_excluded`, `cohort_id`, `ingest_version`) plus `data_version` and the point's `h3_r0`. No defaults for `radius_km`, `sampling_design`, `disease_ascertainment_excluded`, `cohort_id`; the existing strict pandera schema validates at write time, so a violation is a build failure, never a dropped row.

**carrier_observations**. PK `source_record_id`. `CARRIER_OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA`: `carriers`, `n_individuals` in place of `ac`/`an`, same geography and ascertainment columns. Separate table, never unioned with `observations`.

**populations** (P0). PK `population_id`. `lat`, `lon`, `uncertainty_radius_km` (>0, no default), `location_type` (`sampling|ancestral|inferred`), `provenance`, `biocultural_notice`, `registry_version` (`RELEASE+sha256.DIGEST`).

**population_aliases**. PK `(source, label)` -> `population_id`. This is the table that makes the web JSON's `population_label` joinable until `population_id` is added to that projection.

**grid_cells**. PK `(h3_index, res)`: `h3`, `h3_r0`, `parent_h3`, `lat`, `lon`, `worldpop_pop`, `grid_source`, `grid_version`. The published WorldPop res-4 rollup, not the 870 MB raster. Required for any population-weighted aggregate and the burden join.

**artifacts**. PK `(variant_id, model_version, data_version)`: every `manifest.json` field as a column (`artifact_format`, `resolution`, `n_cells`, `n_observations`, `support_counts`, `likelihood`, `correlation_range_km`, `lengthscale_sigma`, `prior_frequency_sd`, `measurement`, `target_grid_source/version`, `registry_version`) plus `first_release`, `served`, `withdrawn`, `cells_sha256`.

**release_objects**. PK `(release, path)`: `key`, `bytes`, `sha256`, `media_type`, `in_git`, `sources[]`, `key_reused_from`. Flattened from every committed manifest, so a release diff and the refit selection rule ("does this derived key already exist in any release?") become one SQL statement instead of a script.

**validation_qc** / **crossval_folds**: the gate table and per-fold CV rows, keyed `(artifact_id, run_id)` and `(scheme, fold)`.

`atlas.duckdb` exposes these in schemas `surfaces`, `observations`, `registry`, `releases`, `validation`, so the observation/surface split is the first thing a reader sees.
queries: **Q1. All observations of variant V within 500 km of a point.** `SELECT variant_id, ac, an, radius_km, sampling_design, cohort_id, assay, source, population_id FROM observations.allele WHERE variant_id = 'chr11-5227002-T-A' AND h3_r0 IN (SELECT unnest(h3_grid_disk(h3_latlng_to_cell($lat,$lon,0),1))) AND ST_Distance_Sphere(ST_Point(lon,lat), ST_Point($lon,$lat)) <= 500000;` The `h3_r0` predicate prunes to a couple of partition files before any arithmetic; the exact great-circle filter runs on what survives, and `radius_km` stays a column so a caller can widen to disc overlap (`distance <= 500000 + radius_km*1000`) without a different table. Today the whole observations corpus is ~1 MB of Parquet (9,273 rows), so this is one or two GETs; at 100x (~1M rows, ~60 MB) a per-variant read still touches one `entity=` partition. Prerequisite: the P1 observation store must actually be published. `genomeos/observations/ingest.py` already writes this layout but fitting is not wired to it (refit design 'gap 3'), and the web JSON projection carries no `population_id`, `rsid`, `source` or date fields. Verified: `h3_grid_disk`, `h3_latlng_to_cell` and `ST_Distance_Sphere` all work from the h3 community extension (H3 4.5.0) and the spatial extension; note the spheroid variants take [lat, lon] order.

**Q2. Value of every surface at one H3 cell, across all variants and versions.** `SELECT variant_id, model_version, data_version, res, post_median, q025, q975, support, posterior_contraction, dist_nearest_obs_km FROM surfaces.cells WHERE h3_r0 = h3_cell_to_parent($cell, 0) AND h3_index IN ($cell, h3_cell_to_parent($cell, 3)) ORDER BY post_median DESC;` The res 3 (v1/v2) to res 4 (v3) mapping is an `h3_cell_to_parent` call, not a join table — the reason the resolution ladder belongs in a column rather than separate file pyramids. **Measured** on the re-encoded layout: 1,713 B of partition metadata + 859,459 B from the single matching partition, 2 of 93 files opened, all 30 served variants returned with seven value columns. On the layout published today the same question costs ~30 x 2.85 MB = ~85 MB, because each file is one row group of 77,844 rows. This query alone justifies the re-encode.

**Q3. Observations for V joined to the population registry.** `SELECT o.*, p.lat AS pop_lat, p.lon AS pop_lon, p.uncertainty_radius_km, p.location_type, p.provenance, p.biocultural_notice FROM observations.allele o LEFT JOIN registry.populations p USING (population_id) WHERE o.variant_id = $v;` A 1,821-row (today) to ~3,500-row (P0 done-when) dimension table that DuckDB broadcasts: one GET for the registry file, one partition for the observations. The join is a LEFT JOIN because sources that carry their own coordinates (MAP surveys, `registry_version = 'map-survey-coordinates-v1'`) keep `o.lat/o.lon/o.radius_km` as authoritative — the registry is never silently substituted. Two small prerequisites: publish a P0 `populations.parquet` + `population_aliases.parquet` release (none exists anywhere today), and add `population_id` to the observation projection. Until then the fallback is `population_aliases` on `(source, population_label)`, which is exactly what that table is for.
design: cost.cost:
**Now: $0-3/month, none of it idle.**
- Storage: 0.27 GB data store + ~0.15 GB web bucket + ~0.15 GB of new derived tables = ~0.6 GB. At ~$0.020/GB-month that is ~$0.012, and the Always Free 5 GB-month Standard tier (aggregated over us-east1/us-central1/us-west1; our bucket is us-east1) covers it. Effectively **$0**.
- Egress at $0.12/GiB with 100 GB/month free from North America: one full release download is 0.27 GB ≈ $0.03. 200 full downloads = 54 GB — inside the free tier if North American, ~$6.50 if not. Website sessions are ~0.43 MB gzip on the critical path; 10,000 sessions ≈ 4.3 GB ≈ $0.52. SQL queries on the pruned layout are ~0.9 MB each; 10,000 ≈ 9 GB ≈ $1.08.
- Class B operations: $0.0004/1,000 after 50,000 free. A pruned query is 5-10 GETs, so 100,000 queries ≈ 1M GETs ≈ $0.40.
- Compute: **$0**. No instance, no Cloud Run, no query service. Fits run on GitHub-hosted runners; the catalog and table build is one deterministic step in `build_data_release.py`.
- The derived tables add storage, not egress — they replace reads that currently cost 30-60x more bytes.
